# Exercise 3: Stroke prediction {.unnumbered}

## Introduction

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Prerequisites: Python libraries"}
This exercise uses the following Python libraries:

- [**torch**](https://pytorch.org/) — for tensor operations (used throughout the course).
- [**pandas**](https://pandas.pydata.org/) — for loading tabular data.
- [**matplotlib**](https://matplotlib.org/) — for plotting (used in the optional appendix).

If any of these are not installed, run `pip install torch pandas matplotlib` in your terminal.
:::

In the previous exercises, we built generative models by specifying the probabilities by hand, using physical laws (heredity) or domain intuition (fraud). In practice, we rarely know the right probabilities. Instead, we **learn them from data**.

This exercise bridges the gap. We will:

1. **Design** two competing graphical models for stroke prediction: a **causal model** and a **naive Bayes model**.
2. **Estimate** their kernels from a real medical dataset.
3. **Sample and predict**: sample from the joint distribution and use rejection sampling to compute predictions from the causal model, and compare with the naive Bayes model's exact posterior.
4. **Evaluate** both models on held-out test data.

The key insight is that **model structure matters**: even with the same data, different graphical models can give dramatically different predictions, and understanding *why* teaches us about the trade-offs between model complexity and data requirements.

### The dataset

We use the [Stroke Prediction Dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/fedesoriano/stroke-prediction-dataset), which contains medical records for 5110 patients. We have split the data into a **training set** (4088 patients) and a **test set** (1022 patients).

The original dataset has been pre-processed into five discrete variables:

| Variable | Values | Encoding |
|----------|--------|----------|
| `age` | young, middle, senior | 0, 1, 2 &ensp;(boundaries: 35, 65) |
| `smoking` | non-smoker, smoker, unknown | 0, 1, 2 |
| `hypertension` | no, yes | 0, 1 |
| `heart_disease` | no, yes | 0, 1 |
| `stroke` | no, yes | 0, 1 |

The prepared data files are:

- [stroke_train_prepared.csv](../data/exercise-3/stroke_train_prepared.csv) — training data (4088 patients)
- [stroke_test_prepared.csv](../data/exercise-3/stroke_test_prepared.csv) — test data (1022 patients)

If you want to learn how the data was prepared from the raw dataset (including loading, exploring, binning, and encoding), see the [optional appendix](#optional-data-preparation).

## Tasks

### Task 1. Design a graphical model

Before touching the data, we think about **model structure**: which variables should depend on which? We will compare two models:

#### Causal model

**Task 1a.** Consider the five variables above. We will use the following causal structure for the rest of this exercise:

- **Generators** (root variables):
    - $\mathsf{age} : I \kernel \text{Age}$
    - $\mathsf{smoking} : I \kernel \text{Smoking}$
- **Kernels** (conditional distributions):
    - $\mathsf{hyp} : \text{Age} \kernel \text{Hyp}$
    - $\mathsf{heart} : \text{Age} \otimes \text{Hyp} \kernel \text{Heart}$
    - $\mathsf{stroke} : \text{Age} \otimes \text{Hyp} \otimes \text{Heart} \otimes \text{Smoking} \kernel \text{Stroke}$

Draw the **string diagram** for this model. Then explain briefly why each dependency might make sense from a medical perspective. Why is `smoking` a root variable rather than a child of `age`? Why does `stroke` depend on all four other variables?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}

[Causal model string diagram to be added.]

- **Age** and **smoking** are modeled as root variables (generators) because they are largely *exogenous*, not caused by the other medical conditions in the model. While smoking rates do vary with age in the general population, this is a demographic correlation rather than a causal effect: age does not *cause* someone to smoke in the way it causes hypertension. Treating them as independent roots keeps the model simple.

- **Hypertension depends on age** because blood pressure tends to rise with age due to arterial stiffening, one of the strongest and best-established risk factors.

- **Heart disease depends on age and hypertension** because cardiovascular damage accumulates over time, and chronically high blood pressure is a primary driver of heart disease.

- **Stroke depends on all four variables.** Age, hypertension, and heart disease are well-established direct risk factors for stroke. Smoking contributes independently: it damages blood vessels and promotes clotting regardless of whether it has already caused hypertension or heart disease.

Note that smoking does *not* appear as an input to the hypertension or heart disease kernels, even though it contributes to both in reality. Including it would increase kernel sizes without much benefit given our limited data.
:::

The causal model's stroke kernel has $3 \times 2 \times 2 \times 3 = 36$ input combinations, so we need to estimate a conditional distribution for each one from our ~4000 training patients.

#### Naive Bayes model

A classic simplification is the **naive Bayes** model, which reverses the direction: instead of features causing stroke, we treat `stroke` as the root and model each feature as depending *only* on stroke status:

- A **generator** $\mathsf{prior} : I \kernel \text{Stroke}$ producing the stroke variable.
- Four **feature kernels** $g_1, \ldots, g_4$, each mapping stroke status to one feature:
    - $g_1 : \text{Stroke} \kernel \text{Age}$, $\;g_2 : \text{Stroke} \kernel \text{Smoking}$, $\;g_3 : \text{Stroke} \kernel \text{Hyp}$, $\;g_4 : \text{Stroke} \kernel \text{Heart}$.

**Task 1b.** Draw the string diagram for the naive Bayes model.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}

[Naive Bayes string diagram to be added — the key structure is: the generator $\mathsf{prior}$ produces $\text{Stroke}$, which is copied four times, and each copy is fed into one of the four feature kernels $g_1, g_2, g_3, g_4$.]

:::

**Task 1c.** Compute the **joint distribution** $p(\text{stroke}, \text{age}, \text{smoking}, \text{hyp}, \text{heart})$ represented by the naive Bayes string diagram. Evaluate the diagram using the composition rules from the course notes.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Interpret the diagram as iterated copy-composition: the generator $\mathsf{prior}$ produces a measure on $\text{Stroke}$, which is then copy-composed with each feature kernel in turn. Equivalently, you can derive the same factorization by repeated application of the chain rule.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}

We evaluate this as iterated copy-composition (equivalently, by repeated application of the chain rule). Copy-composing the generator $\mathsf{prior}$ with $g_1 : \text{Stroke} \kernel \text{Age}$ gives:
$$
(\mathsf{prior} \odot g_1)(s, a) = \mathsf{prior}(s) \cdot g_1(a \mid s).
$$

Copy-composing again with $g_2 : \text{Stroke} \kernel \text{Smoking}$:
$$
(\mathsf{prior} \odot g_1 \odot g_2)(s, a, k) = \mathsf{prior}(s) \cdot g_1(a \mid s) \cdot g_2(k \mid s).
$$

Repeating for all four feature kernels:
$$
p(s, a, k, h, d) \;=\; \mathsf{prior}(s) \;\cdot\; g_1(a \mid s) \;\cdot\; g_2(k \mid s) \;\cdot\; g_3(h \mid s) \;\cdot\; g_4(d \mid s),
$$

where $s$ = stroke, $a$ = age, $k$ = smoking, $h$ = hyp, $d$ = heart. This is the **naive Bayes factorization**: the joint distribution is a product of the prior $\mathsf{prior}(s)$ and four independent likelihoods, each conditioned only on stroke status.
:::

**Task 1d.** Using the joint from Task 1c, derive the **posterior** $p(\text{stroke} = 1 \mid \overline{\text{age}}, \overline{\text{smoking}}, \overline{\text{hyp}}, \overline{\text{heart}})$, the probability of stroke given observed feature values. What happens to the formula when some features are **not observed**?

This situation arises naturally in a diagnostic setting: a doctor may know a patient's age and blood pressure but not yet have their full medical history. A useful model should still be able to estimate stroke risk from whatever information is currently available.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Condition by fixing the observed values and normalizing. For unobserved features, think about what happens in the string diagram when you **delete** an output wire: copying then deleting gives the identity ($\cp \then \del = \id$), and composing a kernel with delete gives delete ($g_j \then \del = \del$), since kernel rows sum to 1.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}

Starting from the joint:
$$
p(s, a, k, h, d) = \mathsf{prior}(s) \cdot g_1(a \mid s) \cdot g_2(k \mid s) \cdot g_3(h \mid s) \cdot g_4(d \mid s),
$$
we condition on all observed values and normalize over stroke status $s$:
$$
p(s \mid \bar{a}, \bar{k}, \bar{h}, \bar{d})
\;=\; \frac{\mathsf{prior}(s) \cdot g_1(\bar{a} \mid s) \cdot g_2(\bar{k} \mid s) \cdot g_3(\bar{h} \mid s) \cdot g_4(\bar{d} \mid s)}{\sum_{s'} \mathsf{prior}(s') \cdot g_1(\bar{a} \mid s') \cdot g_2(\bar{k} \mid s') \cdot g_3(\bar{h} \mid s') \cdot g_4(\bar{d} \mid s')}.
$$

Now suppose only a subset of features are observed. In the string diagram, marginalizing over an unobserved output $X_j$ corresponds to **deleting** that wire. But each wire passes through a copy and then a kernel $g_j$: copying then deleting does nothing ($\cp \then \del = \id$), and composing a normalized kernel with delete gives $g_j \then \del = \del$ (since rows sum to 1). So the entire branch for an unobserved feature vanishes.

If the observed features are $\{j_1, \ldots, j_m\}$, the posterior simplifies to:
$$
p(s \mid \bar{x}_{j_1}, \ldots, \bar{x}_{j_m})
\;=\; \frac{\mathsf{prior}(s) \prod_{k=1}^{m} g_{j_k}(\bar{x}_{j_k} \mid s)}{\sum_{s'} \mathsf{prior}(s') \prod_{k=1}^{m} g_{j_k}(\bar{x}_{j_k} \mid s')}.
$$

Unobserved features simply drop out of the product. This is a key advantage of the naive Bayes model: **partial observations are handled for free**.
:::

### Task 2. Estimate the kernels

Each box in the string diagrams represents a kernel $f : X_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes X_k \kernel Y$. To use the model, we estimate every kernel from training data: count how often each output value $y$ occurs for each input combination $(x_1, \ldots, x_k)$, add 1 for **Laplace smoothing**, and normalize:
$$
\hat{f}(y \mid x_1, \ldots, x_k) \;=\; \frac{\#\{i : Y_i = y,\; X_{1,i} = x_1,\; \ldots,\; X_{k,i} = x_k\} + 1}{\#\{i : X_{1,i} = x_1,\; \ldots,\; X_{k,i} = x_k\} + |Y|}
$$

where $|Y|$ is the number of output categories. Laplace smoothing ensures no outcome receives probability zero. Without it, a single unseen combination would force the entire product to zero. We will see later in the course that this has a Bayesian justification: it corresponds to placing a uniform prior on the probabilities.

**Task 2a.** Load the training data from [`stroke_train_prepared.csv`](../data/exercise-3/stroke_train_prepared.csv). How many patients are in the dataset? How many had a stroke?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
import torch
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("../data/exercise-3/stroke_train_prepared.csv")
print(f"Patients: {len(df)}")
print(f"Strokes:  {df['stroke'].sum()} ({df['stroke'].mean():.1%})")
df.head()
```

:::

**Task 2b (optional — challenging).** Implement a function `estimate_kernel(df, input_cols, output_col, input_sizes, n_output)` that estimates a kernel from the data using the Laplace-smoothed formula above. *If you prefer, you may skip this task and use the implementation provided in the solution below.*

It should return:

- A **kernel tensor** of shape `(*input_sizes, n_output)` where entry `[x1,...,xk, y]` is the estimated $\hat{f}(y \mid x_1, \ldots, x_k)$.
- A **counts tensor** of shape `(*input_sizes)` with the number of training cases per input combination (before smoothing).

For a generator (no inputs), return a probability vector of shape `(n_output,)` and the total count.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint"}
**Counting approach:** Create a zero tensor of shape `(*input_sizes, n_output)`. For each row in the DataFrame, increment `raw[x1, ..., xk, y]` by 1. You can do this with a loop over rows, or vectorized using `torch.Tensor.index_put_` with `accumulate=True`. Then apply Laplace smoothing: add 1 to every cell, and divide by (row total + $|Y|$).

**Generator case:** When `input_cols` is empty, just count how often each output value appears and normalize.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
def estimate_kernel(df, input_cols, output_col, input_sizes, n_output):
    """Estimate a kernel from data with Laplace smoothing.

    Args:
        df:          DataFrame with integer-encoded columns
        input_cols:  list of input column names (empty for generators)
        output_col:  output column name
        input_sizes: number of categories for each input variable
        n_output:    number of output categories

    Returns:
        kernel: tensor of shape (*input_sizes, n_output) with
                kernel[x1,...,xk,y] = estimated P(Y=y | X1=x1,...,Xk=xk)
        counts: tensor of shape (*input_sizes) with training counts
                per input combination (before smoothing)
    """
    cols = input_cols + [output_col]
    sub = df[cols].dropna()

    if len(input_cols) == 0:
        raw = torch.zeros(n_output)
        for y in range(n_output):
            raw[y] = (sub[output_col] == y).sum()
        total = int(raw.sum().item())
        return (raw + 1) / (total + n_output), total

    shape = list(input_sizes) + [n_output]
    raw = torch.zeros(shape)
    idx = [torch.tensor(sub[c].astype(int).values) for c in input_cols]
    idx.append(torch.tensor(sub[output_col].astype(int).values))
    raw.index_put_(idx, torch.ones(len(sub)), accumulate=True)

    counts = raw.sum(dim=-1).int()
    kernel = (raw + 1) / (counts.unsqueeze(-1) + n_output)
    return kernel, counts
```

:::

```{python}
nb["smoking"] = estimate_kernel(df, ["stroke"], "smoking", [n_stroke], n_smoking)

```

Every feature kernel has shape $(2, k)$, with two rows (stroke=0, stroke=1):

```{python}
feature_names = {
    "age": ["young", "middle", "senior"],
    "smoking": ["non-smoker", "smoker", "unknown"],
    "hyp": ["no", "yes"],
    "heart": ["no", "yes"],
}

for name, labels in feature_names.items():
    kernel, counts = nb[name]
    print(f"{name} | stroke  (shape {tuple(kernel.shape)}):")
    print(f"  categories: {labels}")
    print(f"  stroke=0: {kernel[0]}  (n={counts[0].item()})")
    print(f"  stroke=1: {kernel[1]}  (n={counts[1].item()})")
    print()
```

Every NB kernel is estimated from the same two groups: ~3889 non-stroke and ~199 stroke patients. In contrast, the causal stroke kernel splits the data across 36 combinations, some with very few cases.
:::

**Task 2d.** Compare the sample sizes between the two models. Which model has more data per kernel estimate? Why? What are the consequences for estimation reliability?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}

The **naive Bayes** model conditions every feature kernel on stroke alone ($|S| = 2$), so each row is estimated from all ~3889 non-stroke or all ~199 stroke patients.

The **causal** model's stroke kernel conditions on four parent variables with $3 \times 2 \times 2 \times 3 = 36$ combinations, sharing the same ~4000 patients unevenly. Some combinations may have fewer than 20 data points, making those estimates unreliable.

The trade-off: the naive Bayes model has stable estimates but assumes features are conditionally independent given stroke, which is wrong (e.g., age causes hypertension, which causes heart disease). The causal model captures these dependencies but pays a price in data requirements.
:::

### Task 3. Sample and predict

We now use the estimated models to predict stroke risk for individual patients.

For the **naive Bayes** model, we derived a closed-form posterior in Task 1d, so we can compute exact predictions. For the **causal model**, exact conditioning on *partial* evidence is harder (it requires marginalizing over unobserved variables). Instead, we use the same approach as in Exercise 2: **sample from the joint distribution, then filter**. This is rejection sampling, and it works for any graphical model regardless of its structure.

**Task 3a.** Implement a function `predict_nb(evidence, nb)` that computes $p(\text{stroke}=1 \mid \text{evidence})$ using the naive Bayes posterior from Task 1d. The function should accept a dictionary of observed features, allowing partial evidence (unobserved features are simply omitted from the dictionary).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint"}
For each stroke status $s \in \{0, 1\}$, compute the unnormalized score: $\text{score}[s] = \text{prior}[s] \times \prod_{j \in \text{observed}} \text{kernel}_j[s, x_j]$. Then normalize: $p(\text{stroke}=1) = \text{score}[1] / (\text{score}[0] + \text{score}[1])$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
def predict_nb(evidence, nb):
    """Compute P(stroke=1 | evidence) using the naive Bayes model.

    Args:
        evidence: dict mapping feature names to integer values,
                  e.g. {"age": 2, "hyp": 1}. Unobserved features omitted.
        nb:       dict of estimated NB kernels.

    Returns:
        P(stroke=1 | evidence) as a float.
    """
    prior, _ = nb["prior"]
    score = prior.clone()  # shape (2,): one entry per stroke status
    for name, value in evidence.items():
        kernel, _ = nb[name]
        score *= kernel[:, value]  # multiply by g_j(value | s) for each s
    return (score[1] / score.sum()).item()
```

:::

**Task 3b.** Implement a function `sample_causal(causal, N)` that draws `N` samples from the **joint distribution** of the causal model by **sampling according to the structure of the string diagram**: sample each variable in the left-to-right order of the diagram, feeding parent values into child kernels.

In Exercise 2, you sampled from the credit card model by calling each box function following the causal structure of the string diagram. The same idea applies here, except the boxes are *estimated kernel tensors* rather than hand-specified functions. Use `torch.distributions.Categorical` to sample from each kernel.

The key pattern: if a kernel `k` has shape `(*input_sizes, n_output)`, then `k[parent_values]` selects the conditional distribution for each sample. For example, if `hyp_k` has shape `(3, 2)` (one row per age category), then `hyp_k[age]` gathers the right row for each of the `N` samples, producing a tensor of shape `(N, 2)` that `Categorical` can sample from.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Follow the left-to-right order of the string diagram:

1. Sample the two generators (`age`, `smoking`), which have no parents.
2. Sample `hyp` given `age`.
3. Sample `heart` given `age` and `hyp`.
4. Sample `stroke` given all four parents.

Return a dictionary mapping variable names to tensors of shape `(N,)`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
from torch.distributions import Categorical


def sample_causal(causal, N):
    """Draw N samples from the causal model by sampling according to the string diagram.

    Args:
        causal: dict of estimated kernels from Task 2.
        N:      number of samples.

    Returns:
        dict mapping variable names to integer tensors of shape (N,).
    """
    age_k, _ = causal["age"]
    smoking_k, _ = causal["smoking"]
    hyp_k, _ = causal["hyp"]
    heart_k, _ = causal["heart"]
    stroke_k, _ = causal["stroke"]

    # Generators (no parents)
    age = Categorical(probs=age_k).sample((N,))
    smoking = Categorical(probs=smoking_k).sample((N,))

    # Downstream variables (index into kernel with parent values)
    hyp = Categorical(probs=hyp_k[age]).sample()
    heart = Categorical(probs=heart_k[age, hyp]).sample()
    stroke = Categorical(probs=stroke_k[age, hyp, heart, smoking]).sample()

    return {"age": age, "smoking": smoking, "hyp": hyp,
            "heart": heart, "stroke": stroke}
```

Each line mirrors a box in the string diagram: generators produce root variables, and each downstream kernel receives its parent values as indices. The vectorized indexing `hyp_k[age]` selects one row per sample, so no Python loop is needed.
:::

**Task 3c.** Use rejection sampling to estimate $p(\text{stroke}=1 \mid \text{evidence})$ from the causal model, and compare with the exact naive Bayes predictions.

The following `rejection_sample` function is similar to the one from Exercise 2 (see there for a detailed explanation). The main difference is that it takes a `sample_fn` argument, making it reusable across different models.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Provided: `rejection_sample` function"}

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
def rejection_sample(sample_fn, evidence, target, N):
    """Estimate P(target | evidence) by rejection sampling.

    Args:
        sample_fn:  function that takes N and returns a dict mapping
                    variable names to tensors of shape (N,).
        evidence:   dict mapping variable names to observed values,
                    e.g. {"age": 2, "hyp": 1}.
        target:     dict mapping variable names to target values,
                    e.g. {"stroke": 1}.
        N:          number of samples to draw.

    Returns:
        estimate:        estimated probability P(target | evidence).
        acceptance_rate: fraction of samples matching the evidence.
    """
    samples = sample_fn(N)

    # Keep samples that match all evidence
    mask = torch.ones(N, dtype=torch.bool)
    for var, val in evidence.items():
        mask &= samples[var] == val

    n_accepted = mask.sum().item()
    acceptance_rate = n_accepted / N

    if n_accepted == 0:
        return float("nan"), 0.0

    # Among accepted samples, compute fraction matching target
    target_mask = torch.ones(n_accepted, dtype=torch.bool)
    for var, val in target.items():
        target_mask &= samples[var][mask] == val

    return target_mask.float().mean().item(), acceptance_rate
```

:::

```{python}
}

N = 500_000
sample_fn = lambda N: sample_causal(causal, N)

print(f"{'Scenario':<25s}  {'Causal':>10s}  {'Accept%':>9s}  {'NB (exact)':>11s}")
print("-" * 60)

for label, evidence in scenarios.items():
    p_causal, acc = rejection_sample(sample_fn, evidence, {"stroke": 1}, N)
    p_nb = predict_nb(evidence, nb)
    print(f"{label:<25s}  {p_causal:>10.4f}  {acc:>8.2%}  {p_nb:>11.4f}")
```

**Observations:**

- **Scenario B:** Both models agree on near-zero stroke risk for young healthy patients.

- **Scenario C (partial evidence):** Both models handle this naturally. The naive Bayes formula drops unobserved features. Rejection sampling simply filters on fewer variables, so more samples are accepted.

- **Scenario A (the key discrepancy).** The causal model predicts a substantially lower probability than the naive Bayes model.

    **Why?** In the **causal model**, the rejection-sampled estimate reflects how often strokes actually occur among synthetic patients with this exact combination of risk factors.

    In the **naive Bayes model**, each feature independently contributes a likelihood ratio favoring stroke: seniors are more likely to have strokes (age ratio), hypertensive patients are more likely (hyp ratio), patients with heart disease are more likely (heart ratio), and smokers slightly more likely (smoking ratio). These ratios **multiply**. But the features are correlated: age *causes* hypertension, which *causes* heart disease. The naive Bayes model counts the effect of age three times: once directly, once through its effect on hypertension, and once through its effect on heart disease. This **double-counting** inflates the posterior.

    The causal model avoids this because its structure captures the dependencies between variables. When we sample and filter, correlated risk factors are not counted multiple times.

- **Acceptance rates.** Notice how the acceptance rate drops as we condition on more variables (Scenario A vs. C). For rare combinations, we may need more samples to get reliable estimates. This is a fundamental limitation of rejection sampling that we will revisit later in the course.

:::

### Task 4. Evaluate on the test set

**Task 4a.** Load the test data from [`stroke_test_prepared.csv`](../data/exercise-3/stroke_test_prepared.csv). For every test patient, compute the predicted stroke probability using both models. Then report the **average predicted probability** for:

- Patients who actually had a stroke.
- Patients who did not have a stroke.

Does each model assign higher average probability to actual stroke patients?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint"}
For naive Bayes, use `predict_nb` with all four features. For the causal model, rather than calling `rejection_sample` separately for each of the 1022 test patients (which would be slow), sample one large batch from the causal model and compute the stroke rate for each of the 36 unique input combinations. Then look up each test patient's combination.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Note: Direct kernel lookup"}
Since each test patient has values for *all* four input variables of the stroke kernel, one could also read off $p(\text{stroke} \mid \text{age}, \text{hyp}, \text{heart}, \text{smoking})$ directly from the estimated kernel tensor without any sampling. We will see in the chapter on conditioning why this makes sense. Here, we use the sampling approach because it works in general, including for partial evidence where not all parent values are observed.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
test = pd.read_csv("../data/exercise-3/stroke_test_prepared.csv")
print(f"Test set: {len(test)} patients, {test['stroke'].sum()} strokes"
      f" ({test['stroke'].mean():.1%})")
```

For the NB model, we use the exact formula. For the causal model, we sample a large batch and compute the stroke rate for each unique combination of parent values:

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
# Sample a large batch from the causal model
N_eval = 1_000_000
samples = sample_causal(causal, N_eval)

# For each unique (age, hyp, heart, smoking) combo, compute P(stroke=1)
causal_lookup = {}
for a in range(n_age):
    for h in range(n_hyp):
        for d in range(n_heart):
            for k in range(n_smoking):
                mask = ((samples["age"] == a) & (samples["hyp"] == h) &
                        (samples["heart"] == d) & (samples["smoking"] == k))
                n_match = mask.sum().item()
                if n_match > 0:
                    causal_lookup[(a, h, d, k)] = (
                        samples["stroke"][mask].float().mean().item())

# Compute predictions for each test patient
nb_probs = []
causal_probs = []

for _, row in test.iterrows():
    a = int(row["age"])
    h = int(row["hypertension"])
    d = int(row["heart_disease"])
    k = int(row["smoking"])

    nb_probs.append(predict_nb(
        {"age": a, "smoking": k, "hyp": h, "heart": d}, nb))
    causal_probs.append(causal_lookup.get((a, h, d, k), float("nan")))

test["nb_prob"] = nb_probs
test["causal_prob"] = causal_probs
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
stroke_mask = test["stroke"] == 1

print(f"{'Group':<20s}  {'NB':>10s}  {'Causal':>10s}  {'Count':>6s}")
print("-" * 52)
for label, mask in [("Actual stroke=1", stroke_mask),
                    ("Actual stroke=0", ~stroke_mask)]:
    nb_mean = test.loc[mask, "nb_prob"].mean()
    ca_mean = test.loc[mask, "causal_prob"].mean()
    print(f"{label:<20s}  {nb_mean:>10.4f}  {ca_mean:>10.4f}  {mask.sum():>6d}")
```

Both models assign higher average predicted probability to actual stroke patients, confirming they have learned useful patterns from the data.
:::

**Task 4b.** Reflect on the comparison between the two models:

- Which model's predictions are more **spread out** (larger gap between the two groups)?
- Which model's probabilities are more **realistic** (well-calibrated)?
- When might you prefer one model over the other?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}

The **naive Bayes** model typically shows a wider separation between the two groups. However, as we saw in Task 3c, its probabilities tend to be inflated due to double-counting of correlated features. The wider gap partly reflects this overconfidence rather than genuinely better discrimination.

The **causal model** produces more realistic (better-calibrated) probabilities but with noisier estimates, since the stroke kernel splits the data across 36 input combinations.

**When to prefer each model:**

- **Naive Bayes** is the better choice when the goal is *ranking* patients by risk (e.g., deciding who to screen first), when data is limited, or when simplicity matters. It's fast, easy to implement, and its estimates are stable. It also gives exact answers via a closed-form formula.
- The **causal model** is preferable when *calibrated probabilities* matter (e.g., communicating risk to a patient), when you have enough data for reliable kernel estimates, or when you want to reason about *interventions*, e.g., "what would happen to this patient's stroke risk if we treated their hypertension?" The causal structure supports this kind of reasoning; the naive Bayes model does not. The cost is that predictions require sampling, which introduces noise, though this becomes negligible with enough samples.

:::

## Optional: Data preparation {#optional-data-preparation}

The prepared data files used in this exercise were created from the raw [Stroke Prediction Dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/fedesoriano/stroke-prediction-dataset). The original dataset contains 11 columns including continuous variables (`age`, `avg_glucose_level`, `bmi`) and additional categorical variables (`gender`, `ever_married`, `work_type`, `Residence_type`). The raw data files are:

- [stroke_train.csv](../data/exercise-3/stroke_train.csv) — raw training data (4088 patients)
- [stroke_test.csv](../data/exercise-3/stroke_test.csv) — raw test data (1022 patients)

The steps below show how to go from the raw data to the prepared files used in the main exercise. We focus on the five medically relevant variables and discard the rest.

### Step 1. Load and inspect the raw data

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint: Working with pandas"}
[pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org/) is a Python library for working with tabular data. If you've never used it before, there is a 10-minute introduction in the [user guide](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/index.html). Here are the operations you will need:

- **Load a CSV file:** [`pd.read_csv(path)`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.read_csv.html) returns a `DataFrame`, a table with named columns.
- **Inspect the first rows:** [`df.head()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.head.html) shows the first 5 rows.
- **Number of rows:** `len(df)` returns the number of rows.
- **Column data types:** [`df.dtypes`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.dtypes.html) lists the type of each column.
- **Missing values:** [`df.isnull().sum()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.isnull.html) counts missing entries per column.
- **Value counts:** [`df["col"].value_counts(normalize=True)`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.value_counts.html) returns the fraction of each value.
- **Unique values:** [`df["col"].unique()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.unique.html) returns the distinct values in a column.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{python}
#| code-fold: false
import pandas as pd

raw = pd.read_csv("../data/exercise-3/stroke_train.csv")
raw.head()
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
print(f"Patients: {len(raw)}")
print(f"Strokes:  {raw['stroke'].sum()} ({raw['stroke'].mean():.1%})")
missing = raw.isnull().sum()
print(f"\nMissing values:\n{missing.to_string()}")
```

The dataset has 4088 patients, of whom 199 (~4.9%) had a stroke. The only column with missing values is `bmi` (201 missing). Since we will not use `bmi` in this exercise, this is not a concern.
:::

### Step 2. Discretize age

The `age` column is continuous. Since our graphical model framework works with finite sets, we need to **bin** it into categories. We first look at its distribution:

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 2))
ax.hist(raw["age"].dropna(), bins=30)
ax.set_xlabel("age")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Age is roughly uniformly distributed across the range. Based on standard medical thresholds, we bin into three categories:

| Category | Range | Encoding |
|----------|-------|----------|
| young | $[0, 35)$ | 0 |
| middle | $[35, 65)$ | 1 |
| senior | $[65, \infty)$ | 2 |

35 separates young adults from middle-aged patients. 65 is the standard threshold for "senior" in medical literature.

We use [`pd.cut()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.cut.html) to assign each value to a bin:

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
raw["age_bin"] = pd.cut(
    raw["age"], bins=[0, 35, 65, float("inf")],
    labels=[0, 1, 2], right=False
).astype(int)

print(raw["age_bin"].value_counts().sort_index())
```

:::

### Step 3. Simplify smoking status

The raw `smoking_status` column has four levels: "never smoked", "formerly smoked", "smokes", and "Unknown". We merge "formerly smoked" and "smokes" into a single "smoker" category (the distinction between current and former smokers is less important than whether a patient has any smoking history), and keep "Unknown" as a separate level, since it represents genuinely missing information.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
print("Raw smoking categories:")
print(raw["smoking_status"].value_counts().to_string())
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
smoking_map = {
    "never smoked": 0,     # non-smoker
    "formerly smoked": 1,  # smoker
    "smokes": 1,           # smoker
    "Unknown": 2,          # unknown
}
raw["smoking"] = raw["smoking_status"].map(smoking_map).astype(int)

print("\nSimplified smoking (0=non-smoker, 1=smoker, 2=unknown):")
print(raw["smoking"].value_counts().sort_index())
```

:::

### Step 4. Assemble the prepared dataset

We select the five variables, integer-encode them, and save to CSV. The binary variables `hypertension`, `heart_disease`, and `stroke` are already integer-encoded (0/1) in the raw data.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
prepared = raw[["age_bin", "smoking", "hypertension", "heart_disease", "stroke"]].copy()
prepared.columns = ["age", "smoking", "hypertension", "heart_disease", "stroke"]

prepared.head(10)
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
# Verify all values are valid integers
for col in prepared.columns:
    print(f"{col}: {dict(prepared[col].value_counts().sort_index())}")
```

To save the prepared data (and repeat for the test set):
```python
prepared.to_csv("../data/exercise-3/stroke_train_prepared.csv", index=False)
```

The same steps applied to `stroke_test.csv` produce `stroke_test_prepared.csv`.
:::
